# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

questions.question: Should we key the rate limit on `x-customer-id` so each customer has their own quota, rather than client IP (which breaks behind NATs/shared corporate gateways) or both (which adds complexity without a clear threat model)?

options.label: Yes, key on `x-customer-id` only
options.tradeoff: Simple, accurate per-customer billing, but a single customer can still burst from many origins.
options.description: Each `x-customer-id` gets its own counter.

options.label: No, key on client IP only
options.tradeoff: Avoids relying on a header, but corporate customers behind NATs share one quota and dynamic IPs evade limits.
options.description: Limit per source IP address.

options.label: No, key on both
options.tradeoff: More precise abuse isolation, but doubles counter storage and makes enterprise override logic harder.
options.description: Require both header and IP to match a quota.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists the first open decision as what to key the limit on.
brief.how: This decides whether a single customer can exhaust their own quota, whether shared IPs are a problem, and how enterprise limits are scoped.

questions.question: Should we use a token bucket so scripted integrations can burst cheaply while we still cap sustained load, rather than fixed window (burst at window edges) or sliding window (more Redis ops for marginal gain)?

options.label: Yes, token bucket
options.tradeoff: Good burst tolerance, moderate implementation cost in Redis with Lua/Redis Cell.
options.description: Bucket refills at a steady rate; requests cost tokens.

options.label: No, fixed window
options.tradeoff: Simplest, but allows 2x bursts at window boundaries.
options.description: Count requests in time windows (e.g. per minute).

options.label: No, sliding window
options.tradeoff: Smoothest limits, but more Redis reads/writes and harder to explain to customers.
options.description: Track each request timestamp and count within a rolling interval.

brief.how: This shapes burst behavior, Redis script complexity, and how enterprise customers experience throttling.

questions.question: Should counters live in the existing Redis 7 cluster so all three server instances share one global view, rather than in per-instance memory (which triples effective capacity and lets one hot customer hit every instance)?

options.label: Yes, Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Global consistency across instances, but adds a dependency and network hop per check.
options.description: Use the Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions.

options.label: No, in-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: Fast and no new dependency, but limits are 3x weaker and inconsistent under load-balancer shifts.
options.description: Keep counters locally in each Node process.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists counter location as undecided.
brief.how: This determines whether the limit is global, what happens on instance restart, and the failure-mode question next.

questions.question: Should a rejected client receive HTTP 429 with `Retry-After` and a body explaining they hit the orders rate limit, rather than a generic 503 or a silent queueing delay?

options.label: Yes, 429 with Retry-After
options.tradeoff: Standards-compliant and scripts can back off, but scripts that ignore headers will fail loudly.
options.description: Return 429 Too Many Requests plus clear error message.

options.label: No, generic 503
options.tradeoff: Hides implementation detail, but breaks automated backoff and confuses monitoring.
options.description: Return 503 Service Unavailable.

options.label: No, silently delay/queue
options.tradeoff: No client changes, but request backlog can still overload Postgres and hides the problem.
options.description: Slow down or queue excess requests instead of rejecting.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists rejected client UX as undecided.
brief.what: Decide what the client sees when limited.
brief.how: This affects script integration breakages, monitoring alerts, and enterprise customer communication.
